ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, on a rough horizontal ground is placed a columnar object A whose cross section is a quarter circular arc, the left end of A is close against a vertical wall, and a smooth sphere B is placed between A and the vertical wall. The whole device is in a stationary state. If A is moved slightly to the right and they are still in a stationary state, then (　　)
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: The frictional force of the ground on A decreases

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, on a rough horizontal ground there is placed a column-shaped object A whose cross section is a quarter circular arc, the left end of A is close against a vertical wall, and a smooth sphere B is placed between A and the vertical wall. The whole device is in a stationary state. If A is moved a little to the right and they are still in a stationary state, how does the frictional force of the ground on A change?
ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: The frictional force of the ground on A decreases
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the left side is a vertical wall, and the bottom is rough horizontal ground; object A is placed on the ground, and its cross section contains a quarter circular arc surface rising from the lower left to the upper right, with a vertical side on the right; sphere B is clamped between the left wall and A's rising circular arc surface, the left side of the ball is in contact with the wall, and the lower right side is in contact with A's circular arc surface, and the device is stationary. Reasoning: Since sphere B is smooth, the forces between B and the wall and between B and A are both along the normal direction of the contact surface. Analyze the forces on ball B: gravity is vertically downward, the supporting force of the wall on B is horizontally to the right, and the supporting force of A's circular arc surface on B is obliquely to the upper left. The ball is stationary, so the vertical component of A's supporting force on B balances the ball's weight, and the horizontal component balances the supporting force of the wall. Looking again at object A: the reaction force of B on A is opposite in direction to the supporting force of A on B, obliquely to the lower right; the horizontally rightward component among it needs to be balanced by the static frictional force of the ground on A, so the magnitude of the frictional force of the ground on A is equal to this horizontal component. After A is moved a little to the right, the ball is still restricted by the left wall, and the contact point between the ball and A changes on the quarter circular arc surface, making the direction of the normal force there closer to the vertical direction. In order still to balance the ball's weight by the vertical component of the normal force, the horizontal component required of the normal force becomes smaller. Thus the horizontal action component of B on A becomes smaller, and the static frictional force provided by the ground on A also decreases accordingly.
